..(Monday through Saturday)
Issued at 348 PM EDT SAT OCT 31 2026

The long term opens Monday with an upper-level ridge still over much
of the eastern third of the country, with its ridge axis oriented SE
to NW towards the Great Lakes. Farther upstream, a predominant trough
digs into the Great Basin and Four Corners region of the Southwest.
Through the day the ridge will gradually shift farther east, with
surface high pressure expected over the Delaware area. Aside from a
low possibility of a light shower north of I-64 in the morning,
expect dry conditions across eastern Kentucky under southeasterly
downslope flow, overcast skies, and temperatures in the upper 60s to
low 70s, 5 to 8 degrees above climatological normals. Given the
downslope component, deterministic ECMWF and GFS guidance was blended
in to lower dew points a few degrees below standard NBM guidance.
Under decreasing cloud cover, temperatures are expected to cool into
the upper 40s to low 50s Monday night.

On Tuesday, eastern Kentucky will still sit under the upper-level
ridge, with the axis just east of the forecast area. The incoming
cyclone embedded within the trough will progress east into the
Central Plains Tuesday. Deep southwesterly flow aloft ahead of the
approaching system will advect moisture-rich air northeastward into
our region. By Tuesday afternoon, surface winds veer from
southeasterly to more southerly, and mean PWATs around 1.1 to 1.2
inches will have advected into the area. These levels fall within the
85th to 90th percentiles. With strong southwesterly flow aloft,
temperatures are expected to warm into the mid to upper 70s, 10 to 15
degrees above climatological normals. These temperatures are
supported by the 584 dam 500-mb heights across the area, falling in
the 95th percentile. Clouds and precipitation chances look to
increase through the evening and overnight hours Tuesday into
Wednesday. With incoming clouds providing some insulation, along with
continued southerly winds, expect overnight lows in the upper 50s,
around 15 degrees above normal. The record warm low temperature at
the Jackson Airport for Tuesday night is 59F, established in 2016.

Wednesday, as the cyclone progresses into the Tennessee and Ohio
Valleys, a 40-50 kt LLJ will work over eastern Kentucky. The LLJ will
help PWATs surge between 1.25 and 1.50 inches - firmly within the
90th to 97.5th climatological percentile per NAEFS guidance - leading
to widespread rain chances along with breezy conditions. At present,
the LREF 00Z ensemble suite suggests a 20% chance wind gusts could
exceed 40 mph along the high terrain of Harlan County. In addition,
the ensemble guidance also shows a 10% chance of wind gusts exceeding
40 mph south of Lake Cumberland and the city of Monticello. While
little instability exists, strong low-level moisture convergence may
support a few embedded rumbles of thunder Wednesday afternoon and
evening, along and west of the I-75 corridor. Locally heavy rain
rates are also possible in the southwest portions of the forecast
area, and the WPC has issued a Marginal Risk for Excessive Rainfall
(level 1 of 4) for those areas. Temperatures will continue to run
well above average Wednesday afternoon, reaching the upper 60s to
lower 70s - with mid-70s most attainable across far eastern valleys
before steadier precipitation arrives - roughly 8 to 12 degrees above
normal. Mild conditions persist Wednesday night ahead of the
advancing boundary, with lows staying elevated in the mid to upper
50s.

The surface cold front will already be east of the forecast area by
12Z Thursday, though upper-level support may lag behind. Forecast
confidence remains on the lower side through the end of the workweek
due to notable model spread regarding the evolution of the trough.
Ensemble cluster analysis highlights a stark split: while the GEFS
favors a progressive solution where the system lifts cleanly into
Canada, the majority of the EPS members depict the trough shearing
apart, allowing a secondary closed low to cut off over the Deep
South.

Given the potential for a secondary cutoff circulation to maintain a
trough and moisture feed near the southern Appalachians, the NBM has
maintained shower chances that will gradually taper off from west to
east Thursday through Friday. Thursday will remain mild with
afternoon highs reaching the upper 60s to lower 70s, while overnight
lows range from the lower 50s west to mid-50s east. On Friday,
temperatures in the upper 60s to low 70s will continue the stretch of
above-normal highs through the end of the work week. High pressure
looks to build back into the region Saturday, leading to the return
of quiet weather and seasonable temperatures.
